units.ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
units.lo:
The observable properties of solids and liquids
How heating and cooling can change the state of materials
How scientific thinking helps us solve everyday problems

builtFrom.ci: Observing how materials change helps us make sense of the physical world.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of solids and liquids; How heating and cooling change state; Scientific thinking helps solve everyday problems

s.d: Turn the sealed-bag freezing investigation into a short evidence book, not a typed report. Pairs share an iPad with Book Creator and photograph their sealed water bag before and after a teacher-managed freezer session. Students add the photographs to two pages and record an explanation beside each image. They listen back while inspecting the real frozen bag, then replace any recording that does not match the evidence. End by recording whether the frozen water would fill the bottom of a different container immediately. The response reveals whether students distinguish a solid's own shape from a liquid taking its container's shape.
s.why: Combining close-up evidence with recorded explanations lets students revisit and correct their own ideas about freezing.

diff.support: Provide two photographs and the spoken starter: 'Before freezing I thought...; the evidence now shows...'.
diff.stretch: Include partly frozen water and explain how solid and liquid can exist together in the same bag.

s.quote: L1 - What clues help us classify a material as a solid or a liquid?
s.link: This captures observations from Freeze it and uses them to revisit students' original solid and liquid explanations.

s.d: When does an ice cube stop looking like a cube? Pairs share an iPad with Stop Motion Studio open beside a small tray of ice. Keep the device still and take one photo every thirty seconds while students watch and discuss the real ice. Play the captured photographs as a short, sped-up sequence, rather than moving or drawing anything. Replay the moment when solid ice and liquid water are both visible. Students record a spoken before-and-after claim for the teacher, showing that melting changes the state rather than making the water disappear.
s.why: A sped-up record makes gradual melting visible and lets students replay the evidence instead of relying on memory.

diff.support: Give pairs a fixed camera position and a spoken starter describing the ice before and after.
diff.stretch: Compare two equal ice cubes in different locations, keeping the photo interval and containers the same.

s.quote: L2 - How does temperature cause a material to change?
s.link: This adds replayable evidence to the planner's hands-on investigation of ice melting.

s.d: A melted piece of chocolate can become solid again, but will its old shape return? After observing the real material, pairs share an iPad and open FlipaClip. Students draw a short animation showing solid chocolate gradually becoming liquid inside a bowl. They add a cooling sequence showing the chocolate setting in a different-shaped mould. Play the sequence forwards and discuss which changes could happen in the classroom. Finish with students pointing to evidence that returning to the solid state does not mean returning to the original shape.
s.why: Students can animate and replay a proposed change, making the difference between changing shape and changing state visible.

diff.support: Provide three frame prompts: solid chocolate, partly melted chocolate, and liquid chocolate in the container.
diff.stretch: Add a cooling sequence that returns the chocolate to a solid with a different shape.

s.quote: Are all changes caused by heat reversible?
s.link: This builds on heating chocolate by separating a reversible state change from recovering an object's original shape.

s.d: Can a computer tell a solid from a liquid just by looking? Open Teachable Machine in one teacher-run browser tab on the front screen and make two image classes. Groups supply webcam examples of solid objects and water in clear containers, keeping faces out of view. Train the model, then students test unfamiliar examples, including a solid that fits its container. Students check its guesses by observing whether each material keeps its own shape when moved between containers. Finish by naming a wrong guess and the physical evidence that settles it.
s.why: A live classifier gives students a reason to test whether appearance alone provides enough evidence to identify solids and liquids.

diff.support: Provide the spoken starter: 'It looks like a liquid, but our container test shows...'.
diff.stretch: Test the same material in different containers and explain why the computer changes its prediction.

s.quote: L1 - What clues help us classify a material as a solid or a liquid?
s.link: This extends Sunken shapes by making students check visual guesses against observable properties.

s.d: Bring the class's melting results together in one Microsoft Excel sheet on the front screen, run by the teacher. Pairs test equal ice cubes in matching trays in two classroom locations, checking at the same intervals. Students report the minutes until no solid ice remains, and the teacher enters each pair's results. Insert a column chart so everyone can compare repeated tests rather than one winning result. Check the class predictions against the chart and identify which location would keep ice solid longer. Listen for students using evidence, rather than simply saying that shade is always colder.
s.why: A live class chart brings repeated results together so students can spot patterns and question surprising measurements.

diff.support: Provide a paper results table with labelled columns for location and minutes until the ice melts.
diff.stretch: Identify an unusual result and propose a repeat test that keeps ice size and observation intervals consistent.

s.quote: L3 - How can understanding heat and materials help us in real life?
s.link: This uses the planner's ice investigations to compare evidence for an everyday cooling decision.

stem.d: Allow about fifteen minutes to gather cardboard, foil, fabric scraps, matching containers, sealed ice bags and Micro:bits for groups of four. Each group builds an ice shelter and uses one shared computer, with MakeCode open in a web browser, to program a Micro:bit to display temperature when button A is pressed. Keep the board dry beside the sealed ice bag, explaining that it measures the board's temperature, not the ice itself. Students compare readings and visible ice remaining at regular intervals against an uninsulated container, keeping ice amounts and test times equal. They improve one part of the shelter and repeat the test, demonstrating whether their change kept more ice solid.
stem.why: Live temperature readings help students compare shelter designs alongside direct observations of how much ice remains.

diff.support: Provide matching containers and a simple labelled sketch showing where to place the sensor and sealed ice bag.
diff.stretch: Change only the lid design, then repeat the test with equal ice and the same starting conditions.

stem.quote: L3 - How can understanding heat and materials help us in real life?
stem.link: This turns the planner's cooling investigations into a practical design task using evidence to slow melting.

units.ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
units.lo:
The ways people use technology to express their creativity.
How texts and images work together.
How technology influences our creativity.

builtFrom.ci: Creativity allows people to express their understanding of the world.
builtFrom.lo: The ways people use technology to express creativity; How texts and images work together; How technology influences our creativity

s.d: Does a picture keep its meaning when its caption changes? Open Adobe Express in a web browser, with pairs sharing a device. Using one teacher-provided playground photo, students duplicate their design and add a different caption to each version. They compare how the same image can suggest excitement, loneliness or a surprising event. Preparation takes ten minutes to choose the photo and check access. Pairs show both versions to another pair, then revise one caption to make its intended meaning clearer.
s.why: Changing captions while keeping an image fixed makes the influence of words on visual meaning easy to compare.

diff.support: Provide three short captions to choose from and a sentence starter: The words make this image seem.
diff.stretch: Write a caption that deliberately contradicts the image, then ask viewers how they resolved the conflicting messages.

s.quote: How texts and images work together.
s.link: This gives students a direct way to investigate the planned relationship between texts and images.

s.d: How little must a face change before we read a different feeling? Pairs share an iPad running Stop Motion Studio above a paper face with movable eyebrows and mouth. Students photograph small movements to animate a change between two expressions. They replay the sequence and adjust a movement that sends an unintended message. Prepare paper pieces and check camera positioning in ten minutes before a single lesson. End by pausing an unfamiliar pair's animation halfway through, inviting different interpretations supported by visible facial clues.
s.why: Frame-by-frame playback reveals how tiny changes to facial features can change the feeling an audience reads.

diff.support: Provide a paper face outline and movable eyebrows and mouth pieces, with six photographs as the starting target.
diff.stretch: Keep the mouth still and test how much meaning students can communicate by changing only the eyebrows.

s.quote: Facial expression as a form of communication Term 1 - students explore how we communicate and express ourselves using our faces.
s.link: This supports the planned exploration of reading and changing facial expressions through close observation of small movements.

s.d: Bring back the picture book image used in Music. Groups of three share an iPad with GarageBand and record short keyboard parts using notes from their pentatonic work. Students layer the parts, then listen with one part muted to hear what it contributes. They rerecord one part so it better represents a feature such as repeated shapes or movement. Allow two lessons and ten minutes to check recording and playback beforehand. Finish by playing the combined piece while students point to the image features their musical choices represent.
s.why: Recording separate musical parts lets students hear, compare and adjust how their sounds work together to represent an image.

diff.support: Mark three suitable notes on a paper keyboard guide and give each student a clear recording turn.
diff.stretch: Keep the notes unchanged but alter the rhythm of one part to represent a different feature of the image.

s.quote: Music: students worked in small groups to create a composition inspired by a picture book image.
s.link: This extends the planned group composition by letting students record, isolate and improve the musical parts they created.

s.d: Can the same scene feel peaceful and busy? Pairs share an iPad with Brushes Redux and draw a familiar playground using simple shapes and marks. Students take turns trying different colours and brush marks, using undo to compare choices. They keep two versions by saving the first before changing it. Allow one lesson, with five minutes beforehand to check saving works. Finish with a spoken before-and-after claim that shows whether students understand how digital editing can change the feeling of an image.
s.why: Quickly undoing and retrying marks lets students compare creative choices without having to start their artwork again.

diff.support: Give pairs a three-item drawing prompt and split the drawing and observing roles.
diff.stretch: Create a second version using the same shapes but different marks, then test whether viewers interpret it differently.

s.quote: They will learn foundational skills such as taking well-composed photographs with an iPad and using the basic drawing and editing tools in apps like Brushes Redux and PicEdu.
s.link: This builds on the planned exploration of digital art tools by making their influence on students' creative decisions visible.

s.d: One closed cardboard box can look ordinary or mysterious. Pairs share an iPad with IMovie and film three short shots of a box being approached and opened. Students make two short edits from the same footage, changing shot length and adding recorded sound to only one. They play both versions to the class, which identifies the more tense version and cites a specific editing choice. Allow two lessons and ten minutes to gather boxes and check recording. Each pair records a final spoken claim explaining how technology changed the audience's reading rather than the event itself.
s.why: Editing the same footage in two ways makes the effect of timing and sound on dramatic tension immediately audible and visible.

diff.support: Give pairs three prepared object-only clips and a simple editing sequence: trim, reorder, add sound, replay.
diff.stretch: Keep the footage order and sound unchanged, then test whether different shot lengths alone alter the tension.

s.quote: They also learn to analyse dramatic tension through in film and television and how/why certain elements are used.
s.link: This turns the planned analysis of dramatic tension into a practical comparison of students' own editing decisions.

stem.d: Groups of three use cardboard, fabric scraps and tape to build a puppet with a Micro:bit secured behind a window for its LED mouth. Sharing a computer, students open the Micro:bit block editor in a web browser and code buttons A and B to display different mouth patterns. They test whether classmates can distinguish the intended feelings, then improve either the window shape or one light pattern and test again. Finish by demonstrating both working expressions and explaining which facial clues made their meaning clearer. Allow two lessons, with fifteen minutes beforehand to gather materials, check connections and display a simple button-code example.
stem.why: Programmable expressions let students test how a working puppet communicates feelings and improve its physical and digital design together.

diff.support: Provide a cardboard face outline and a printed example of the two button blocks with simple LED patterns.
diff.stretch: Design two expressions that differ by only two lights, then test whether viewers can still distinguish their intended meanings.

stem.quote: They look into the universal facial expressions and further build their understanding on reading expressions and changing expressions to communicate feelings in various situations…
stem.link: This extends the planned work on facial communication into a physical puppet whose changing expressions students can build, control and test.

units.lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

builtFrom.lo:
How needs and wants lead to new inventions
How digital devices and networks operate
Being a responsible digital citizen

s.d: Make an invisible message journey visible with a short animation. Pairs share an iPad with FlipaClip open and draw two classroom devices connected through a wireless access point. Across six to ten frames, students move a coloured message symbol from sender to access point to receiver. Explain that this is a simplified journey between devices on the same classroom network. Pairs replay their animation and record a spoken explanation for the teacher, showing that messages travel through connections rather than jumping straight between screens.
s.why: Animation makes a hidden journey visible, allowing students to replay and check the order of a message travelling.

diff.support: Provide a paper sequence showing sender, wireless access point and receiver for students to draw from.
diff.stretch: Animate a second message travelling back and explain why both devices must send and receive.

s.quote: What happens inside our computers and networks when we send a message or a picture to someone else?
s.link: This turns the planner's question about sending messages into a visible sequence students can check.

s.d: Which classroom problem actually needs an invention, rather than just sounding fun? Pairs identify everyday difficulties, then the class agrees on four problems to investigate. Run one shared Microsoft Excel spreadsheet in a browser on the front screen and enter students' votes beside each problem. Create a column chart, then change the counts as students reconsider after hearing reasons. Students compare the live chart with their initial predictions and name a need their proposed invention would meet.
s.why: A live chart helps students compare competing needs before deciding which problem an invention should solve.

diff.support: Provide three pictured problems and a spoken starter: Our invention would help people to...
diff.stretch: Compare first choices with second choices and explain whether the class should change its priority.

s.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
s.link: This gives the planner's invention question a concrete starting point in students' own classroom.

s.d: A screen, a keyboard and a loose cable are on the table: which parts make a working computer? Pairs share an iPad with Popplet open and photograph safe, disconnected items supplied by IT. They arrange the pictures around a computer picture and connect each part to a short explanation of its job. After a class demonstration, students move pictures and revise connections rather than starting again. Finish with an unfamiliar mouse or speaker so students can explain its function, not just recognise its appearance.
s.why: Movable pictures and connections make students' changing ideas about computer parts easy to compare and discuss.

diff.support: Supply six close-up pictures and three labels: takes information in, processes information, and sends information out.
diff.stretch: Add a touchscreen twice and explain why one component can have both input and output jobs.

s.quote: Create a mind map in Popplet app…
s.link: This extends the planned systems picture sort into a map showing how computer parts work together.

s.d: Turn a familiar online dilemma into a small book classmates can actually navigate. Pairs share an iPad with Book Creator open and choose a fictional situation from the Library's safe versus risky discussions. They create a starting page with two choices and link each choice to a different consequence page. Students add recorded explanations about privacy, kindness or asking a trusted adult for help. Demonstrate linking to a page once on the front screen before students build. Classmates test both routes, then identify which consequence shows that deleting a message does not undo someone already seeing it.
s.why: Linked choices let students test the consequences of online decisions instead of simply listing safety rules.

diff.support: Provide one fictional situation, two possible choices and spoken sentence starters for the consequences.
diff.stretch: Add a choice that seems helpful but shares private information, then explain a safer alternative.

s.quote: Unplugged by Steve Antony sparked discussion about balancing screen time with real-world play and how unplugging from devices can spark creativity and connection, while The Internet is a Puddle by Shona Innes helped students identify safe versus risky online situations - a lesson reinforced through the Safe vs Risky Puddles Seesaw activity.
s.link: This builds on the Library's safe versus risky discussions by letting students explore the consequences of different choices.

s.d: Can two small devices send a signal without a cable joining them? Groups of four share two micro:bits and a laptop with the micro:bit coding editor open in a browser. Model blocks that set the same radio group, send a number when button A is pressed, and display a heart when that number arrives. Students build and download the programs, then test sending across their table. Give each group a different radio group number so tests stay separate. Finish by demonstrating a working connection and explaining why both devices need matching radio settings.
s.why: Sending real radio messages lets students test how shared settings and programmed instructions affect communication between devices.

diff.support: Provide a printed block sequence and assign clear programmer, sender, receiver and recorder roles.
diff.stretch: Change only one device's radio group, predict the result, then restore communication and explain the fix.

s.quote: How digital devices hardware and software operate through and networks specific components, commands, and operate procedures.
s.link: This gives students a working example of hardware following programmed commands to communicate.

stem.d: Could a small delivery robot reliably reach a classroom supply station? Groups of four build a floor-level docking bay from cardboard, recycled containers, tape and popsticks, with an opening wide enough for a Sphero BOLT. Allow about ten minutes to gather materials and mark one shared robot testing lane, with an iPad running its coding controls. Across two lessons, groups take turns programming a short roll-and-stop sequence, testing whether the robot enters without hitting the sides while other groups build. Students keep the starting point and program unchanged, improve one physical guide, then demonstrate whether three repeat runs dock more reliably.
stem.why: A moving robot provides a repeatable delivery test, helping students judge whether their physical design genuinely solves a problem.

diff.support: Provide a flat cardboard base and a drawn parking outline so groups can focus on building side guides.
diff.stretch: Test the dock from a second starting position and improve it without changing the original successful approach.

stem.quote: Why do people invent things, and how do we design a solution for a real problem?
stem.link: This makes the planner's design question tangible as students improve a docking bay to meet a delivery need.

units.ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
units.lo:
Soils, rocks, and minerals have observable properties that make them useful in different ways.
Earth's resources are vital for living things, including humans, and must be used responsibly.
First Nations Australians have long-standing knowledge and cultural uses of soils, rocks, and minerals.

builtFrom.ci: The diversity of soils, rocks, and minerals shapes the way people value and use Earth's resources.
builtFrom.lo: Observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals; Earth's resources are vital and must be used responsibly; First Nations knowledge of soils and rocks

s.d: Where can we see people using the land around them? Open Google Maps in one teacher-controlled browser tab on the front screen, with no student login needed. Spend ten minutes beforehand checking satellite and Street View coverage near Melbourne and an Indonesian location. In one lesson, students direct zooms and walkthroughs, then add observed similarities and differences to the planner's paper Venn diagram. Finish by separating visible evidence from questions needing research, especially whether bare ground shows farming, building or resource extraction.
s.why: Moving between satellite views and street-level scenes helps students connect landforms, vegetation and visible uses of resources.

diff.support: Give pairs three comparison prompts: exposed rock, plant cover and nearby buildings.
diff.stretch: Find a second location that challenges one of the class's first comparisons.

s.quote: Comparison: Students create a Venn diagram or report comparing natural features of Australia with a neighbouring country.
s.link: This gives the planned comparison a shared set of places students can inspect rather than relying only on written descriptions.

s.d: Turn the planned digital presentation into a moving explanation of why soil matters. Pairs share an iPad and open Adobe Express in a web browser to make three short scenes using shapes, arrows and simple animation. Students show rain carrying exposed soil away, then show how losing soil can affect plants and animals. Allow two lessons and ten minutes beforehand to practise animating an arrow. End with a spoken explanation of the sequence, checking that students connect soil loss with living things rather than treating soil as just dirt.
s.why: An animated sequence makes the links between soil, plants and living things visible over time, rather than listing separate facts.

diff.support: Provide three paper planning boxes labelled soil, plant and living thing before students begin animating.
diff.stretch: Add a second sequence showing how keeping soil covered changes the outcome after heavy rain.

s.quote: Design a poster or digital presentation showing how soils, rocks, and minerals are important for life, culture, and the environment across different places.
s.link: This develops the planned presentation into an animated explanation of connections between soil and living things.

s.d: Can two quarries supply the same amount of stone but disturb different amounts of land? Pairs share an iPad running Minecraft Education and build a small grass-covered stone hill in Creative mode. They collect an agreed number of stone blocks, counting surface blocks removed and recording a screenshot. In a second lesson, they rebuild and test a narrower access route before presenting both designs on screen. Allow ten minutes to check world settings, and finish by explaining how equal resource yields can have different land footprints.
s.why: Students can remove and rebuild the same landscape, making the trade-off between obtaining resources and disturbing land easy to inspect.

diff.support: Give pairs a small marked work area and a target of eight stone blocks.
diff.stretch: Keep the same stone target while reducing both disturbed surface blocks and the length of the access route.

s.quote: Earth's resources are vital for living things, including humans, and must be used responsibly.
s.link: This gives the concluding presentation a tested example of how people can change the way they obtain resources.

s.d: Begin with a teacher-selected, community-endorsed First Nations source about ochre or grindstones. Pairs share an iPad and use GarageBand audio recording to capture a short explanation in their own words, naming the source and community. They listen back against the source, then record a corrected second version on another track. Allow two lessons and fifteen minutes beforehand to select the source and check recording. Play the two versions separately so students can hear whether their explanation now includes cultural value, rather than only what the material was used for.
s.why: Listening back to short recordings helps students check that they distinguish a material's practical use from its cultural value.

diff.support: Provide the spoken starters 'The source explains...' and 'This material matters because...' on a small card.
diff.stretch: Identify a question the source does not answer and explain whose knowledge would be needed.

s.quote: Cultural Knowledge: Students explain how First Nations Australians use a particular rock, mineral, or soil resource and reflect on its value.
s.link: This develops the planned cultural explanation through careful listening, source checking and revision, with First Nations voices guiding the content.

s.d: Does a rock look equally rough from every side? Pairs share an iPad with Scaniverse to scan a large, textured rock on the school grounds, leaving it in place. Students move slowly around it, then rotate and enlarge the saved model back inside. Allow one lesson and ten minutes beforehand to check a suitable rock and practise scanning. Finish by comparing the scan with field observations, identifying which visible properties support a possible use and which need hands-on checking.
s.why: A rotatable scan lets students revisit a rock from several angles and check whether their descriptions hold up.

diff.support: Provide a three-word observation bank and assign one student to scan while the other checks coverage.
diff.stretch: Find a feature the scan misses and explain why direct observation is still needed.

s.quote: Rock and Mineral Hunt: observe and describe local rocks (colour, texture, grain, crystal size).
s.link: This extends the rock hunt by giving students a shared object they can revisit when comparing observable properties.

stem.d: In groups of four, students build a soil-saving barrier across a shallow tray slope using pebbles, popsticks and fabric scraps. Each group shares an iPad running IMovie to record a measured water pour and replay the clip at reduced speed, spotting where soil first escapes. Students improve one gap or support, repeat with the same soil slope and water volume, then compare both clips in a two-lesson project. Finish by demonstrating the working fix and explaining how the barrier reduces soil movement. Allow fifteen minutes beforehand to gather trays, small soil samples, catch containers and materials, and practise slowed playback.
stem.why: Slowed video reveals where water first breaks through a barrier, helping students improve a specific weak spot rather than guess.

diff.support: Provide a ready-made tray slope and assign clear builder, water-pourer, recorder and observer roles.
diff.stretch: Test whether the improved barrier still works when the same water volume is poured more quickly.

stem.quote: Local Soil Study: collect soil samples from different locations around the school or local area.
stem.link: This extends the local soil study into building and testing a way to keep valuable soil from washing away.

units.th: Where We Are in Place and Time
units.ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
units.lo:
How Australia and its neighbouring regions define places
First Nations Australians have deep and ongoing connections to Country, which are spiritual, cultural, and environmental.
Places can be understood and valued in different ways, depending on cultural and historical perspectives.

builtFrom.ci: Land and place are represented and valued in different ways.
builtFrom.lo: How Australia and neighbouring regions define places; Australia's states/territories have unique identities; First Nations connections to Country

s.d: Can a close-up of one feature help someone recognise a favourite school place? Pairs share an iPad with Scaniverse to scan a small outdoor feature, such as a garden rock or seat, keeping people out of view. Students move slowly around it, then rotate the finished model to check what was captured. Each pair presents two viewpoints and explains why this feature makes the place meaningful. Classmates compare their responses, revealing that the same place can matter for different reasons.
s.why: A rotatable scan lets students revisit a familiar feature from different angles and point out details that make it meaningful.

diff.support: Give pairs a nearby feature to scan and the spoken starter, 'This place matters to me because…'.
diff.stretch: Find a detail hidden from the first viewpoint and explain how it changes someone's impression of the place.

s.quote: Students can find a favourite place in the JS to capture, paint or sketch.
s.link: This adds a view students can rotate to the planner's exploration of meaningful school places.

s.d: Bring back the original world maps and let students add their learning in a different colour, as planned. Pairs share an iPad and take turns photographing their own updated map in Seesaw. Each student records a short explanation while drawing on the image to highlight Australia, a neighbour and their relative positions. Students replay their recording and check that their spoken directions match the map. End with a before-and-after claim that lets the teacher hear whether students now distinguish a country, a continent and a capital city.
s.activity: Adding to the original world map
s.why: A recorded explanation makes students' map changes audible, revealing whether new labels reflect stronger geographical understanding rather than copying.

diff.support: Give students the spoken sequence, 'I used to think… Now my map shows… My evidence is…'.
diff.stretch: Explain one thing the map still cannot show clearly and suggest another representation that would help.

s.quote: Students are given their original world map and asked to add to it - using a different colour to show new learning.
s.link: This keeps the planner's different-colour map assessment and adds a replayable explanation of the geographical thinking behind each change.

s.d: Does a country that looks close on a world map feel close when you zoom in? Pairs share an iPad and open Google Maps in a web browser, with no student login needed. Students locate Australia and two neighbouring countries, then describe their directions using north, south, east and west. They zoom between the regional map and available Street View locations to investigate coastlines, roads and buildings. Finish by locating an unfamiliar neighbouring country and explaining its direction from Australia, checking compass understanding rather than country-name recall.
s.why: Zooming between regional maps and street-level views connects compass directions with visible features of places students have not visited.

diff.support: Provide a compass card and two named countries for pairs to locate before exploring a street-level view.
diff.stretch: Find a neighbouring country that extends in more than one direction from Australia and justify both directions.

s.quote: Revise the points of the compass. Talk about our Asian neighbours.
s.link: This builds on compass revision by connecting neighbouring countries' locations with views of actual places.

s.d: Before the lesson, select a short, community-endorsed Clickview video featuring a First Nations speaker discussing their own Country. Run one browser tab on the front screen while students listen for spiritual, cultural and environmental connections. Pause at two moments for pairs to discuss what the speaker actually says. Students request a replay to check their evidence, then draw connections between the examples on a shared paper chart. Finish with a spoken claim about why Country means more than a location, naming the speaker's evidence rather than guessing cultural meanings.
s.why: Pausing and replaying a First Nations speaker's explanation helps students ground their ideas about Country in an identified voice.

diff.support: Offer the spoken starter, 'The speaker describes a connection through…', alongside three still images from the selected video.
diff.stretch: Identify one connection that fits more than one category and explain why separating those categories can be misleading.

s.d: Turn the planner's respect-for-place writing into a small model visitors can test. Pairs share an iPad running Minecraft Education and use a flat world to build a simple Australian creek picnic area. Students add a walking route and one protective feature, such as a fence beside fragile plants, then explain whose needs their choices serve. Another pair walks through the model and reports where the intended route becomes unclear. Students rebuild that section and demonstrate the fix, showing how a design can support access while caring for a place.
s.why: Walking through a shared model lets students test whether their proposed ways of caring for a place actually guide visitors.

diff.support: Provide a paper sketch showing a water edge, an entrance and a path for pairs to build.
diff.stretch: Test whether two visitors can pass without leaving the path, then improve the design without widening every section.

s.quote: Choose a place or feature of Australia and write and how and why people could show respect for it.
s.link: This gives students a walk-through model to test before explaining how people could show respect for an Australian place.

stem.t: Build a Creek Crossing That Works
stem.d: With about 15 minutes to gather cardboard, tape, popsticks and low supports, set groups the challenge of crossing a blue-paper creek without blocking it. Groups of four share a Sphero BOLT and an iPad running its control app to build a low bridge wider than the robot. Students program a slow, straight crossing and repeat the same run three times, noting slips, stops or successful crossings. They improve one part, such as the joins or side rails, and retest with the same program. Finish by demonstrating a reliable crossing and explaining how a built structure changes movement across a natural boundary.
stem.why: A programmed robot provides a repeatable crossing test, helping students compare how changes to a bridge affect movement across a boundary.

diff.support: Provide a short, straight driving program and two equal-height supports so groups can focus on the bridge surface.
diff.stretch: Add an approach bend and adjust the driving sequence while keeping the bridge and creek width unchanged.

units.ci: Strategies support healthy relationships and personal growth.
units.lo:
How our words, actions and choices affect others
Ways we can solve problems and manage conflict respectfully
Why is it important to listen to feedback and use it to grow
What helps us keep going when things get tricky

builtFrom.ci: The choices and actions we make contribute to our health and wellbeing.
builtFrom.lo: What it means to be healthy; Choices and their impact on health; Actions to maintain a healthy mind and body

s.d: One friendship problem can lead to two very different endings. Groups of four share an iPad, recording a brief fictional disagreement and two possible responses in IMovie. They assemble two short films using the same opening: one response escalates the problem, while the other follows the sorry flow chart. Keep filming to simple seated scenes so the focus stays on words and actions. Replay the moment where the endings diverge and identify the choice that matters. Each group demonstrates an apology that includes a practical way to make amends.
s.why: Editing two endings onto the same conflict makes the effects of different responses easy to compare and replay.

diff.support: Provide a three-line fictional script and the planner's sorry flow chart beside the recording space.
diff.stretch: Create an ending where an apology needs a practical repair, then show why words alone are insufficient.

s.quote: Going Further Lesson 5: Making amends Practice using the sorry flow chart in pairs…
s.link: This extends sorry flow chart practice by letting students compare the consequences of two responses.

s.d: Bring back a short piece of speaking students have already practised for their learning conversations. Pairs share an iPad and use Seesaw to record a first attempt, followed by one specific piece of spoken feedback. Each student chooses a suggestion, rehearses away from the screen and records a second attempt. Keep both recordings in the same post so students can replay them in order. Students add a final voice explanation naming the advice they used and the evidence of improvement. Listen for a clear connection between feedback, action and growth, rather than simply greater confidence.
s.why: Side-by-side recordings preserve evidence of feedback being used, rather than relying on students remembering their first attempt.

diff.support: Offer the spoken starter: I tried your suggestion to change this because it would help listeners.
diff.stretch: Identify feedback you chose not to use and explain how your goal helped you make that decision.

s.quote: How can I show evidence of my growth?
s.link: This gives the planner's feedback and goal setting work a replayable record of improvement.

s.d: After a challenging group music rehearsal, turn the classroom podcast station into a place to share useful advice. The teacher sets up one shared recorder and microphone while groups of four plan a one-minute conversation away from devices. Each group records what became difficult, which strategy they tried and whether it helped them continue. Other groups rehearse or continue their music while waiting for their turn. Play the recordings through the classroom speakers and ask listeners to identify strategies they could actually use. Finish by choosing one strategy to test at the next rehearsal, making persistence more specific than simply trying harder.
s.why: A short audio recording captures students' actual strategy choices and makes their advice available for classroom listening.

diff.support: Use three spoken prompts: What was tricky, what did you try, and what happened next?
diff.stretch: Explain when your strategy would not help and name a different strategy you could try instead.

s.quote: Students were required to reflect on their group experience, and consider which choices were important for their group to succeed.
s.link: This turns the music reflection into practical, recorded advice about keeping going during a shared challenge.

s.t: Animating a Character with Adobe Express
s.d: Can the same words sound welcoming and unkind? Pairs share an iPad and open Animating a Character with Adobe Express in a web browser. They choose one character and record two short versions of a fictional greeting, keeping the words identical but changing their tone. Play both animations to another pair without revealing the intended meaning. Listeners describe what they heard and which voice clues shaped their judgement. Finish by recording a class claim about why friendly words alone do not always sound friendly.
s.why: Animated voice recordings let students isolate tone and hear how identical words can send different messages.

diff.support: Give pairs the same short sentence and two tone words to try aloud before recording.
diff.stretch: Test a sentence whose meaning stays unclear, then add words that make the friendly intention easier to understand.

s.quote: Goal: To identify and describe friendly behaviour at school.
s.link: This adds a listening comparison to the planner's exploration of friendly behaviour.

s.d: Could two responses to the same Friendship Fire lead to different endings? Pairs share a computer with Canva open in a web browser to build a three-page, clickable comic using a fictional planner scenario. On the opening page, students write two possible responses and link each response to a different ending page. Each ending shows the other character's reaction and whether the problem is resolved. Allow two lessons, with ten minutes beforehand to practise linking text to pages. Pairs present their comic for classmates to click through both paths, then explain why listening and making amends work better than simply saying sorry.
s.why: Clickable choices let students test different responses to the same conflict and discover why a quick apology may not resolve it.

diff.support: Give pairs two response starters: 'I need a moment because…' and 'Can you tell me what happened?'
diff.stretch: Add a response that sounds polite but ignores the problem, then show why the conflict continues.

s.quote: Can you sort out these Friendship Fires? Read all six scenarios and then select two to write about.
s.link: This builds on the Friendship Fire scenarios by letting students create and test contrasting responses rather than describe just one solution.

stem.d: Allow 15 minutes to gather cardboard, tape, string, popsticks and bottle tops, and mark a straight testing lane. Groups of four share an iPad running the Sphero BOLT controls and build a lightweight chariot that the robot can tow with a loose string harness. They run the robot along the same lane at the same speed for the same duration, checking whether the chariot stays upright and carries a small load to the finish. After each test, students give one specific observation, change one part and repeat the run with the same settings. Finish with a working demonstration and a spoken explanation of how feedback helped the group persist and improve its design.
stem.why: Repeatable robot movement helps groups compare chariot changes while practising useful feedback and persistence through real setbacks.

diff.support: Provide a simple folded-card chariot example and assign builder, driver, observer and recorder roles within each group.
diff.stretch: Test whether your improvement still works with a larger load, keeping the route and robot settings unchanged.

stem.quote: Sphero challenge task, Friendship Fire story writing and our Sphero Chariot race.
stem.link: This builds directly on the planner's chariot race, making cooperation, feedback and persistence visible during a practical design challenge.
